items.body: Neram Pularumbol (“As The Dawn Breaks”) finds Sunken Cages pulling the rhythmic traditions of South India into an electronic vocabulary of bass, drones, and fractured club music. The album opens in celebratory, ebullient mode with “Kerala”, before “Elephant Dance” raises the tempo and “Idakka” takes a more synthetic path, processing patterns from the traditional hourglass-shaped Kerala drum. Breath soon becomes almost as important as rhythm. On “Darantee”, featuring Kuza, vocal exhalations and percussion give the music a physicality that draws on the agricultural and folk roots of South India. The connection with Kerala runs throughout the record, particularly through the collective force of its percussion traditions. “Drum and Flowers” imagines Chenda drums within a celebratory night dance, their increasingly animated rhythms rubbing against darker industrial sounds. “Athiraavile” — Malayalam for “early in the morning” or “at the break of dawn” — shifts the scene towards daybreak, combining an unprocessed Chenda melam pattern with heavy electronic beats and Rani Jambak’s incantatory voice. Throughout, traditional instruments remain clearly audible even as their rhythmic properties are stretched, fragmented and repositioned. The second half effectively takes that process apart again through a substantial series of remixes. “Drum and Flowers” alone appears in three new iterations: Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull its rhythmic framework in sharply different directions, at points veering towards acid, jungle and deconstructed club music. The source material consequently keeps changing hands and contexts, with each version exposing possibilities latent in the original. For all its electronic density, Neram Pularumbol eventually circles back towards the physical act of playing. “Kerala (Moki McFly Remix)” brings proceedings to an apt conclusion, returning percussion to a more tactile foreground and introducing distinctly jazzy, free-form leanings. The album begins and ends with “Kerala”, but the intervening transformations ensure that the return doesn’t feel quite like arriving at the same place. photo by Mike Vanemon To find out more about the production process for the album, we got in touch directly with Ravish Momin (aka Sunken Cages). The liner notes to Neram Pularumbol use resynthesis not simply as an electronic process but as a metaphor for taking culture apart into its constituent elements and putting it together differently, in opposition to the idea of tradition as something “frozen, solidified and sanctified”. That does seem particularly audible on Neram Pularumbol, where South Indian instruments and rhythmic languages are present but rarely allowed to function as straightforward markers of heritage. What exactly are you trying to preserve when you dismantle and reconstruct a tradition in this way, and at what point does transformation become more important than recognisability? Does this also connect with what you have described elsewhere as “resynthesizing the traditional” and decolonising conventional ideas of so-called global music? Thanks for this great question! The best analogy to start with is to think of making a photocopy of a photocopy. Even 8-10 generations of copies later, they do not resemble the original, get distorted and warped, and perhaps even a new narrative emerges. This process itself is of deep interest to me and what I’m hoping to preserve. When I think of a rhythm I’ve learned in the past, it’s more about how I’m recalling it in the moment, with all the unconscious inspirations and changes that get added over time- to be left with a transformation that’s an impression, an organic reimagining- similar to what happens to our own memories over time. Furthermore, I’m taking these ‘resynthesized patterns’ and placing them in a new framework of synths, drones, and other electronic elements that I’ve absorbed, to create a new global-music that simply doesn’t rely on invoking the past. I need to be careful to add that all this does not mean a blatant disrespect of the culture and tradition, but to be left with recognizable elements-like the sounds and basic structure of a pattern- in an arrangement that may be unfamiliar. That’s where the decolonizing takes shape. Music is predicated on a dynamic process of growth and evolution, yet too often non-western artists are expected to be performative of their culture, and their use of contemporary technologies or drawing inspirations from western genres is considered disingenuous. Gatekeeping and branding from western ethnomusicologists and curators has a long problematic history, but I’ll leave that discussion for another time Neram Pularumbol is particularly rooted in the musical traditions of Kerala, from the title itself to “Idakka”, named after the hourglass-shaped drum associated with Kerala’s temple music. Yet you don’t present these traditions ethnographically or attempt to reproduce them faithfully: their rhythmic and timbral characteristics are broken apart and absorbed into electronics, bass and club structures. Which particular Kerala musical traditions, instruments or rhythmic practices fed into this album, and what is your own relationship to them? Are there elements that you consciously wanted to retain in recognisable form, and others that you felt could only remain alive by being transformed? Hopefully my previous response lends some insight to this question as well. To elaborate, I’ve always found group drumming to be powerful, an action of resistance and solidarity as well as of spiritual significance. Particularly, I was mesmerized by music performances known as Chenda melam in which hundreds of artists sync and perform together during temple festivals in Kerala. The drums native to Kerala, like the Chenda, Idakka and Elathalam, also have markedly different timbres/sonorities from the North-Indian drums such as Tabla and Dhol to which one may be accustomed to hearing. While I’m originally from South India (Hyderabad) myself, I currently split my time between Brooklyn and Philadelphia. I did not grow up in Kerala, India, but I wanted to think about what a meaningful recreation of those rituals into my own worldview, that was culturally respectful as well, would represent. For example, On “Drum and Flowers,” I created a narrative with shifting tempos where the Chenda drum is used in a celebratory night dance, after the workers have come home. A multitude of drums lead the celebrations, shedding industrial grime for synchronized movements that quicken, a shared bodily memory of ancestral resistance and resilience. The song is punctuated with industrial textures and dark synth stabs that represent the rigor of factory-work. “Idakka,” the track to which you’d alluded earlier, runs the Idakka drum patterns through various delays and echo filters to create this cavernous rhythmic feel where machine-like sounds are also ever-present. Here the traditional elements are drastically transformed and chopped up, signifying a not-too-distant future where machines threaten to take over humanity. On “Athiraavile,” which features the Indonesian producer/vocalist Rani Jambak, I actually used a clean / unprocessed Chenda melam pattern on top of heavy electronic beats. Here, Rani lends a shaman-like call to prayer- not belonging to any specific religious denomination- where people gather to play drums at dawn. The second half of the album effectively allows other artists to take your rhythmic material apart again. “Drum and Flowers” is especially revealing because Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull the same source towards very different rhythmic and electronic environments, while Masma Dream World and Moki McFly produce two strikingly different versions of “Kerala” and Kush Arora makes “Idakka” considerably harsher and more propulsive. You have said that these collaborators were chosen partly through relationships you have built with artists around the world who approach tradition as something mutable rather than fixed. When you heard the finished remixes, did any of them reveal something in your own compositions that you hadn’t realised was there? And does handing the music over to artists from such different cultural and musical contexts become another stage of the album’s idea of resynthesis? The remixes were as much a part of the album as the tracks. And a resounding yes to your observation of having these remixes represent a further reshaping of the source-material, as multiple layers of resynthesis now exist Each artist brought their respective cultural background, musical aesthetic and production style to the table. Back during the pandemic lockdown in 2020, I’d actively sought out remote collaborations with artists in different corners of the globe. I do want to emphasize that it was also important for me to support women artists, do my part to highlight them in a male-dominated electronic music scene. Over the years, I’ve maintained my goal of building a musical community with diverse collaborators who all take musical risks and blend the traditional to the digital in their own practice. As an artist with a remix track-record of my own (Babani Sound System, Batida’s Ikoqwe, Depeche Mode, dragonchild and Thollem), I’ve spent a lot of time listening to a given track to quickly hone in on elements that resonated with my aesthetic- whether it was a vocal phrase, a melody or a rhythmic motif. The objective was to take apart the original track and re-stitch it back together highlighting that chosen element, in ways that wouldn’t be predictable. El Kontessa added a doumbek pattern to the underlying rhythm and made it feel like it was always there, as if South Indian and Egyptian musicians jammed all the time. Masma Dream World took the drone elements of “Kerala” which I’d intentionally layered heavily, to create a very cinematic track with a stripped down minimal beat. Weldroid’s acid synths and bit-crushed elements gave the track a dance music of the future energy. Lila Tirando a Violeta removed my rhythmic elements entirely and energized the track with a Jungle vibe. Moki Mc Fly seemed to instinctively grasp my AACM past- which was grounded in their ancient to the future motto- and brought an acoustic Free-Jazz tribute to the Art Ensemble of Chicago to his remix. Neram Pularumbol means “As The Dawn Breaks”, while the name Sunken Cages itself has a much darker environmental origin: you have described the “sunken cage” as an image of something once held captive becoming submerged by rising waters, reflecting your background in environmental engineering and longstanding concern with climate change. Yet this record often feels less apocalyptic than that image suggests: despite the drones, industrial textures and moments of considerable darkness, there is movement, colour and a sense of emergence. What does “dawn” mean within this record? Is it intended as a counterweight to the darker implications of Sunken Cages, or do you see destruction, transformation and renewal as parts of the same process? For the past few years, I’ve been thinking a lot about the duality of the nature of water, as a source of survival and also as one of destruction. While there is a sense of hopelessness that comes from realizing that some of the impacts of climate-change are irreversible, there is also hope in focussing on environmentally sustainable practices. Rather than thinking of dawn as a counterweight to the bleakness of the overarching climate narrative, I wanted to leave its symbolism ambiguous. In other words, we can meet the dawn feeling powerless or prepare to transform our future for preservation. On a broader level, the choice still doesn’t seem to have been made. As far as the tracks go, I play with the tension between the forces of darkness and rejuvenation- with the industrial sounds/textures on the verge of overpowering the ancient rhythms and chants, which signify our humanity, and certainly different tracks allude to different outcomes of that struggle. PS. Since this interview took place, Momin has released Morning Birds and Distant Drums, a new album with Haitian “soundchemist” Val Jeanty as Turning Jewels Into Water. Taking the AACM credo “Ancient to the Future” as a guiding principle, the record brings their Indian and Haitian lineages into a kinetic dialogue with improvisation and contemporary electronics. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: experimental electronic / global fusion / South Indian percussion / deconstructed club
items._cn_summary: Sunken Cages 的《Neram Pularumbol》以南印度传统节奏体系为素材，通过合成器、贝斯、低频嗡鸣与碎裂化俱乐部音乐语言进行拆解与重组。专辑以庆祝性的《Kerala》开场，随后《Elephant Dance》和《Idakka》分别提速并引入对伊达卡鼓音型的电子化处理；《Darantee》中人声呼吸与打击乐并置，唤起南印度农业与民俗传统的身体感；《Drum and Flowers》将钦达鼓置于节庆夜舞场景，与暗色工业声响形成摩擦；《Athiraavile》则以原始钦达梅拉姆节奏叠加电子重拍与 Rani Jambak 的吟唱式人声。专辑后半段以多组混音重构同一素材，呈现酸曲、丛林与解构俱乐部等不同方向。最终《Kerala (Moki McFly Remix)》回归打击乐的触觉质感，引入自由爵士式倾向，形成首尾呼应但非简单重复的整体弧线。

items.body: Review by Logan — The ambient, coolly nostalgic opening sequence of Geogaddi indicates the record's direction. Adjusting to the full album required some acclimation after years of listening to Music Has the Right to Children, but many elements appealed to me right away. Taking some distance from the debut allowed this strange, isolated world to make sense."Music Is Math" and "1969" rely on steady, ticking beats reminiscent of the D�sseldorf electronic scene, but with an uneasy feeling underneath. Further into the tracklist, pieces like "The Beach at Redpoint", "Gyroscope", and "Alpha and Omega" shift toward a darker Krautrock friction. The record relies on hypnotic, repetitive loops rather than traditional musical showmanship, focusing on old-sounding, distorted analog textures.My first favourite was clearly Music Has the Right to Children, which I found immediately accessible, followed by The Campfire Headphase, though I still loved Geogaddi during that era. However, it was only after Inferno came out that I deeply loved the final three albums, and the early material became more distant to me. This record is more like a 4.5 for me, though it gets a rounded-down 4 for Prog Archives purposes. Geogaddi is a strong exercise in sound design, but it remains a step below those late-career masterpieces for me. Inferno, The Campfire Headphase, and Tomorrow's Harvest mean the most to me these days, but all of Boards of Canada's albums I consider to be masterpieces in their own ways.Key tracks for me: "The Beach at Redpoint" and "Music is Math".
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以冷调的怀旧氛围开场，构建出一个孤立而陌生的声场。节奏部分借鉴杜塞尔多夫电子场景的稳定脉动，表面规整却暗藏不安。深层曲目转向更暗沉的推进感，依靠催眠式的重复循环和失真模拟纹理推进，摒弃传统炫技，以声音设计为核心。模拟设备的老旧质感贯穿全作，与前作的明亮易接受形成对比，需要时间适应。评论者将这张专辑视为他们成长中重要但不及后期作品亲密的阶段，虽给出四星但内心定位在四星半，认为它是声音设计的扎实练习，关键词是《The Beach at Redpoint》和《Music Is Math》。

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Is CARDIACS a progressive rock band? The question, which may have sparked debate at one time, seems obsolete today. All we can say is that singer and guitarist Tim Smith?the band's longtime leader, its heart, mind, and soul, and now more than ever regarded as an exceptional English artist, more than five years after his passing?is a child of the vibrant prog universe that truly lives up to its name. He himself cited among his countless influences such legendary names as Genesis, Faust, Can, Gong, Zappa, and Gentle Giant?a fact confirmed by the album *A Little Man And A House And The Whole World Window*.From the very introduction of the excellent new version of the track "A Little Man and a House," it becomes clear that this album will be on an entirely different level than *Seaside*, their previous album released in 1983. The compositions date back to the previous three years, but the production is much richer than on *Seaside* and in no way tainted by the typical sound of the '80s. Musically, it's a true leap forward, with arrangements of unprecedented richness ("The Icing on the World"), sometimes bordering on unnecessary excess ("The Breakfast Line," saved by its impressive grand finale). The significant contribution of William D. Drake's keyboards (who joined the band in late 1983) is no small part of this, as the musician displays a boundless imagination that rivals Tim's. Drake also co-wrote two of the album's most progressive tracks: "I'm Eating in Bed," which appears as a bonus track?a surreal little nursery rhyme that could easily have fit on *Nursery Cryme* or *Foxtrot*; and "The Whole World Window," which closes the album in a rather unexpected way, bringing CARDIACS closer to King Crimson's *In The Court* with heavy use of mellotron, piano, and bombastic organ, thereby convincing us once and for all that this is one of the most important prog works of 1988.
items._cn_summary: 这是英国前卫摇滚乐队 Cardiacs 1988 年发行的代表作，融合了 Genesis 的叙事结构、Faust 与 Can 的实验精神、Zappa 的怪诞编排以及 Gentle Giant 的复杂和声。专辑较前作在制作上实现了质的飞跃，编曲密度极高且层次丰富，键盘手 William D. Drake 的加入为作品注入了极具想象力的器乐色彩。他与 Tim Smith 共同创作的两首曲目尤为突出：一首带有超现实童谣气质，呼应早期 Genesis 的奇幻美学；另一首以键盘群为核心，结尾处大量运用柔音琴、钢琴与管风琴，向 King Crimson 致敬。整张专辑在结构与情绪上不断切换，兼具戏剧性与怪趣，被视为 1988 年最重要的前卫摇滚作品之一。

items.body: An ache moves forward He steps back I step forward It all turns black He steps forward I step back Some relationships develop their own terrible choreography: one person advances, the other retreats, and a moment of contact sends both back through the same steps. On Annihilate, underground post-industrial producer and vocalist Lana Del Rabies gives that exhausted dance a setting of metallic percussion, dissonant strings, and voices that seem to drift through the walls. The prospect of closeness carries a threat of disappearance, as though reaching for another person might cost you the outline of yourself. Released through her own Feral Crone Recordings, the single revisits the gothic industrial territory of her 2023 album STREGA BEATA. Among her most accessible recordings to date, Annihilate brings its melody into clearer view within a dense, unsettling arrangement, with echoes of mid-career Nine Inch Nails, early Chelsea Wolfe, Dead Can Dance, and Godflesh. Written and produced by Lana Del Rabies, the track features bass, guitar, and additional instrumentation from Zach Wise, formerly of experimental black metal band Hissing. Deeply reverberant string tones open the song, their discord setting the room askew before a soft metallic beat begins carrying it forward. Creaking noises punctuate the haze, while thudding distortion stays buried beneath the mix, suggesting a heartbeat accelerating at the approach of something unwelcome. Her singing is soft, breathy, and eerily close; farther away, wails stretch across the recording like cries attempting to reach the living. The whole thing suggests a deserted Victorian factory, its decaying rooms still occupied by machinery and something considerably harder to identify. That dusty, corroded atmosphere recalls the gothic industrial aesthetics of the 1990s, with every small sound acquiring an uncomfortable physical presence. The lyrics begin with images converging in reverse and a moment suspended in time. From there, the exchange becomes a sequence of opposing movements: his withdrawal prompts her advance, his approach sends her backward. “Push pull fade” reduces the relationship to its recurring mechanism. Hearing her name briefly promises recognition, but the next attempt at contact leaves her grasping in vain. By the time the title enters the refrain, desire reads as a force capable of wearing away the person who feels it. Directed and edited by Lana Del Rabies/Sam An, the video translates that instability into grainy woodland footage, overlapping figures, and close-ups that dissolve before they can offer much certainty. Pale dresses and fabric catch the light against dense foliage; raised arms, blurred faces, and bodies close to the ground recur through successive layers of exposure. Black-and-white images give way to smeared color, turning the setting into something resembling a damaged reel of folk horror. The footage was shot by Jane Slater, whose video credits include Dildox, Brood Faye, and Sacred Skin, and Vox Porter of Sleek Teeth. Watch the video for Annihilate below: Lana Del Rabies began with early experiments sampling female pop musicians into noise tracks, a practice reflected in the project’s name. An has since developed a body of work spanning industrial music, gothic electronics, and experimental heaviness, examining human brutality and the prospect of apocalypse. Her recordings have earned attention from The Quietus, Metal Hammer, and Anthony Fantano, while her live performances have taken her to festivals including Roadburn, Coldwaves, Sled Island, Prepare the Ground, Northwest Terror Fest, and Soulcrusher. She has toured with Author & Punisher, 3TEETH, Pharmakon, JPEGMAFIA, and John Wiese, and opened shows for artists including clipping., Midwife, HEALTH, and Bell Witch. In 2025, An founded the art-focused label Feral Crone Recordings and released Le Temps Viendra and Omnipotent Fuck. She is currently working on a studio record with former members of Hissing, due in 2027. Listen to Annihilate below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: Lana Del Rabies 以单曲《Annihilate》延续其哥特工业路线，由她自己创办的地下厂牌 Feral Crone Recordings 发行。歌曲以金属打击乐、不协和弦乐与仿佛穿墙而过的幽魂人声构建出一种逼近消失的关系：一方前进一步、另一方便退后一步，渴望本身被书写为一种磨损自我的力量。混音中低频失真若隐若现，如心跳逼近某种不祥之物；飘远的哀号则像是试图触达生者的呼喊。整首曲子呈现出一座维多利亚时代废弃工厂的质感：腐朽的空气里仍有机器的低鸣，与九十年代哥特工业美学遥相呼应。乐评将其与 Nine Inch Nails、Chelsea Wolfe、Dead Can Dance、Godflesh 并置，指出旋律在密集的不安编曲中获得了相对清晰的轮廓，是她迄今最具可听性的作品之一。MV 由 Lana Del Rabies 与 Sam An 执导，将这种关系的不稳定感转化为颗粒感强烈的林间影像，叠加的人影与不断溶解的特写呼应着歌中那份触而不得的徒劳。

items.album: Wrocław 2026
items.excerpt: On 1 October 2026, Nachtmahr chose Poland to open the longest and largest tour in the project’s history: three consecutive club dates in Wrocław, Poznań and Warsaw, with Cygnosic and Bagger 258 joining the opening run before IMPERIVM continues further across Europe. items.body: On 1 October 2026, Nachtmahr chose Poland to open the longest and largest tour in the project’s history: three consecutive club dates in Wrocław, Poznań and Warsaw, with Cygnosic and Bagger 258 joining the opening run before IMPERIVM continues further across Europe. When Thomas Rainer and I spoke ahead of the tour, he admitted that beginning in Poland had originally been a logistical decision, but previous experience with Polish audiences made it an unexpectedly appropriate one. A new programme inevitably introduces a degree of uncertainty, and he expected the energy of the Polish crowd to remove it very quickly. Wrocław supplied a fairly emphatic confirmation. Three bands approached electronic physicality from markedly different directions, yet there was no weak transition between them. Bagger 258 worked through blunt rhythmic force, aggressive vocals and a very direct relationship with the dancefloor; Cygnosic loosened that geometry into something darker, broader and more fluid; Nachtmahr then inherited a room already fully activated and pushed it into a much less orderly state. The evening did not feel like a headliner plus obligatory support. Its construction mattered. And Wrocław really is being spoiled this autumn. The number of strong dark-electronic, industrial and gothic concerts passing through the city has reached the point where they are beginning to form a genuine season rather than a handful of unrelated bookings. This was another very persuasive addition. Bagger 258 Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil I should already have seen Bagger 258 at the NCN Warm-Up this year, but unfortunately missed them there, so Wrocław finally gave me the chance to catch up. It took very little time to understand what I had missed. The Augsburg duo, Nico von der Eisenmühle and Tim “Hacke” Schmelzer, released their debut album “Aufwärts gehts bergab” in February 2026. Its language places them firmly inside EBM: Arbeiterwut, Funktion, Kontrolle!, Werkshalle 4, “Körperkommando“, Schicht im Schacht. Machinery, work, discipline and repetitive physical action are everywhere in the imagery, while Nachtmahr themselves contributed a remix of “Werkshalle 4” to the record. Live, however, Bagger 258 were far more interesting than a catalogue of genre references might suggest. Their greatest strength was immediacy. The beats came down hard and square, the vocals had real abrasion to them, and yet the performance never became rigid. There was too much visible enjoyment onstage for that. The music was aggressive, but the aggression kept converting itself into movement. There is a considerable difference between performing the visual grammar of old-school EBM and actually making a room respond to it. Bagger 258 did the latter. The pulse was almost mechanically regular, but the communication around it was human, animated and frequently playful. They were not protecting a historical form. They were using it. For an opening band, they also did exactly what an opening band should do without ever seeming subordinate to what followed. The audience did not require a long negotiation before deciding whether it was ready to move. Bagger 258 established that physical vocabulary almost immediately, and by the end of the set the room had already shifted from people waiting for the main act into people actively participating in the evening. Rainer had told me before the tour that the right support band changes the condition in which a headliner encounters its audience. If someone else has already brought the room to a certain level, you do not have to begin from zero. Bagger 258 made the point rather convincingly. Absolute knockout. Cygnosic Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Cygnosic changed the type of pressure rather than reducing it. The Athens project of Georgios Psaroudakis has a long history within dark electro, with Psaroudakis writing, performing and producing the material himself. “Demystify”, released in 2023, was Cygnosic’s seventh full-length album, while 2025’s “Theorem” reconstructed existing Cygnosic pieces through metal arrangements and showed how naturally heavier structures can sit inside the project’s electronic identity. That breadth could be felt live. Compared with the harder edges of Bagger 258, Cygnosic sounded more fluid and spacious, but describing it simply as “gentler” would undersell what was happening. The force had merely changed direction. Instead of striking repeatedly at the centre, the arrangements seemed to spread across the room, gathering weight through layers, melody and continuity. There was more air inside the music and more room for individual elements to develop. The rhythms still carried the performance, but the relationship between rhythm and atmosphere was different. Movement became less regimented, more continuous. The set could be forceful without constantly attacking. That made Cygnosic particularly effective in the middle position. Bagger 258 had already established the body as the evening’s main point of communication; Cygnosic kept the body engaged while changing how it moved. The result was dynamic, dark and surprisingly graceful. It also prevented the three-band bill from becoming three variations on the same impact. By the time Cygnosic finished, the audience was still physically engaged but had travelled through a noticeably different emotional texture, leaving Nachtmahr with exactly the kind of room Thomas Rainer had spoken about before the tour: warmed up, responsive and ready to be pushed considerably further. Nachtmahr Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil When Thomas Rainer and I spoke for Side-Line in August, much of our conversation circled around a contradiction at the centre of Nachtmahr live. The project’s visual language is built from command, discipline, uniforms, hierarchy, severity and theatricalised authority. Producing that world requires enormous control: sound, lighting, costumes, movement, timing and musicianship all have to function together. Yet the result Nachtmahr seeks from the audience is almost the exact opposite. The crowd is invited to abandon restraint, surrender to rhythm and lose control inside something that has been very carefully controlled on its behalf. For Rainer, the construction starts with the songs themselves. As he told me then, “The setlist is the script for the movie we present every night on tour.” The first IMPERIVM show gave that sentence a much more concrete meaning. The album, released on 26 June 2026 through Trisol, develops methods Rainer had already begun testing on “Verboten!” rather than simply applying another layer of production to an established Nachtmahr template. In our interview, he described Verboten! not as the end point of an evolution but as the record that established the method for what followed. IMPERIVM takes that logic further while retaining the project’s unmistakable rhythmic and visual identity. Onstage, however, theory disappears very quickly behind physical action. Thomas Rainer commands a room in a way relatively few performers can. That is not simply another way of saying that he is charismatic. What impressed me was how actively he reads the response in front of him. A gesture produces a reaction; he catches that reaction and sends it back, larger. The next rhythmic hit strengthens it again. The relationship becomes circular rather than one-directional. In Wrocław, that feedback loop escalated with remarkable speed. The entire live formation is central to why it works. Nachtmahr no longer reads as one central figure surrounded by secondary decoration. There are several simultaneous points of attention across the stage, and the movement between them gives the performance much of its tension. The musicians maintain the structural discipline, while the women in the production are integral to the stage language rather than simply ornamental additions. Their choreography, posture and interaction reinforce Nachtmahr’s play with authority and submission. They contribute to the sense of order, but also to its deliberate instability. The more precisely the stage is arranged, the more excessive the activity in front of it can become. And the audience went completely wild. Not “wild” merely because people were dancing hard. What happened was cumulative. The room became denser at the front, hands were constantly raised, bodies moved forward, and the separation between active participants and passive spectators progressively disappeared. Every successful exchange with the stage seemed to authorise a larger response. That is why “madness” is both tempting and slightly inadequate as a description. The apparent madness had an architecture. It was being built. Rainer had explained in our interview that his band and crew remove much of the need for conscious control once he is onstage, allowing him to respond instinctively and become absorbed in the energy coming back from the room. He wanted the same for the audience: a framework reliable enough that people could safely lose themselves inside it. “I have a wonderful band and crew who take the need for control out of my hands, so I can completely let go onstage and simply become one with the energy of the crowd.” Wrocław demonstrated exactly what he meant. Bagger 258 and Cygnosic had already brought the audience a considerable distance. Nachtmahr did not have to spend the opening part of the set manufacturing involvement. They could begin by directing something already in motion. From there, the room became increasingly feral. One of the most striking aspects of a Nachtmahr show remains this gap between what the imagery appears to promise and what the live experience actually produces. Onstage there is hierarchy, command and discipline; in front of it, the effect is strangely collective. The imagery separates roles, while the music dissolves them. People move together. The stricter the construction onstage became, the less restrained the audience appeared. And in the middle of all that force came one of the evening’s most delicate moments. Thomas Rainer took time to remember Witek Kopytko, our colleague and a deeply valued member of the scene, who passed away earlier this year. He distributed tiny toy horses among people in the audience in Witek’s memory. It was a small, personal gesture, but precisely because nothing about it was inflated into spectacle, it carried real emotional weight. For those of us who knew Witek, worked alongside him or simply shared this scene with him over the years, the moment briefly changed the emotional temperature of the room. The concert had been built around movement, control and physical intensity; suddenly there was space for affection and remembrance. It was a genuinely beautiful tribute to a colleague who is very much missed. It also said something important about what these scenes actually consist of. Bands, promoters, journalists, photographers and audiences may occupy different roles at an event, but over years those roles begin to overlap into a community. Remembering one of its people in the middle of such a large production was not a detour from the evening. It belonged there. When the music resumed, the contrast only made the final part of the set more pronounced. The machinery returned, the crowd returned to movement, but the evening had briefly revealed something much softer underneath it. The setlist Rainer’s description of the setlist as dramaturgy becomes particularly interesting when looking at the stage sheet from Wrocław. New IMPERIVM material was not placed into an isolated promotional block; it sat among songs from different periods of Nachtmahr’s catalogue. With the clearly crossed-out alternatives on the photographed sheet omitted, the visible running order was: Wer Wind sät, Keine Lieder, Weil ich’s kann!, Liebst du mich?, Tanzdiktator, Stärker als ihr Hass, Sirenen, Heile mich, Die Straße, Kampfbereit, Beweg dich!, “Mädchen in Uniform“, Unterwerfung, Der Schlaf, Katharsis. Ending on “Katharsis” was especially fitting. By that stage, the idea had already been enacted physically for well over an hour. Wrocław, and what comes next There was something especially satisfying about watching all of this happen here. Wrocław has been remarkably well served by dark music this autumn, and the concentration of good bookings is beginning to change the rhythm of the city’s scene. It matters that international industrial, EBM, darkwave and gothic artists are not simply appearing as occasional exceptions but arriving regularly enough for audiences to develop continuity between events. That continuity is important because nights like this depend on difference as much as similarity. Bagger 258 took familiar EBM mechanics and made them feel immediate, aggressive and highly physical rather than nostalgic. Cygnosic widened that physicality into something more fluid, melodic and atmospheric. Nachtmahr then absorbed everything accumulated during the previous sets and used it as raw material for a performance based on reciprocal escalation. The Polish IMPERIVM opening continues with Poznań at Pod Minogą on 2 October and Warsaw at VooDoo Club on 3 October, before the tour moves on internationally. Audience in Wrocław Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil About Nachtmahr, Cygnosic and Bagger 258 Bagger 258 are an Augsburg-based German EBM duo formed by Nico von der Eisenmühle and Tim “Hacke” Schmelzer. Their debut album “Aufwärts gehts bergab” was released in February 2026 and includes remixes by Nachtmahr, NordarR and Menticide; Side-Line covered the album in a March 2024 interview with the duo. Cygnosic is the Athens-based dark-electro project of Georgios Psaroudakis. “Demystify” appeared in 2023 as the project’s seventh full-length album, while 2025’s “Theorem” revisited Cygnosic compositions through metal arrangements without abandoning the project’s electronic core. Side-Line first covered the Nachtmahr connection in 2019, when Cygnosic toured with Nachtmahr and labelmates C-lekktor behind the “Epiphany” LP. Nachtmahr, founded by Austrian musician Thomas Rainer in 2007, has developed a distinctive language around hard electronic rhythm, theatrical authority, confrontation, discipline and increasingly broad stylistic freedom. IMPERIVM is the latest stage of that development, while the current tour is the largest and longest undertaken under the Nachtmahr name. The Wrocław opening showed how carefully the three-band construction worked: Bagger 258 established the body, Cygnosic changed the way it moved, and Nachtmahr took control of what had already been set in motion. By the end, the contradiction Thomas Rainer and I had discussed before the tour, extreme control on one side of the stage and deliberate surrender on the other, no longer needed explaining. It was visible everywhere in the room.

items.body: This album from the Danish project Black Vault was actually released quite some time ago—back in the spring of 2025. With the telling title “Death Obsessed”, we are presented with five tracks. There is no room for fun in this sonic universe; instead, we are confronted with a dark, nihilistic-sounding whole. The atmosphere is carefully constructed and accentuated by occasional spoken-word samples, creating a tormented listening experience. Blending elements of Dark-Ambient, Industrial, Noise, and even Ritual music, the production is sometimes a tiny chaotic yet undeniably well-crafted. The combination of influences is fascinating, and, to my mind, the opening two tracks are particularly compelling. Black Vault transports us into an illusory world of ruin. The only thing missing, for me, is an absolute climax—though that certainly doesn’t mean this isn’t a great record. (Rating:7½). Listen to “The Hollow Sighs Of Putrid Emission”: The Hollow Sighs Of Putrid Emission by Black Vault About Black Vault Black Vault is a Danish project working in occult industrial and death-industrial territory on the German label Dunkelheit Produktionen. The project’s debut album, “Hymns To The Great Devourer”, was released on Dunkelheit Produktionen in 2023. “Death Obsessed” is the follow-up, recorded between 2023 and 2024 and released on March 1, 2025, mixed and mastered by Grant Richardson at Hex Audio Labs.
items._cn_summary: 丹麦项目 Black Vault 的第二张专辑《Death Obsessed》由德国地下厂牌 Dunkelheit Produktionen 发行，收录五首作品。整张专辑呈现出黑暗、虚无主义的声场氛围，通过精心构建的氛围层次与零散出现的spoken-word 采样交织，制造出极度压抑的聆听体验。制作人将Dark-Ambient、Industrial、Noise乃至Ritual音乐的元素熔于一炉，编排虽偶显混乱却整体做工精良，尤其前两首曲目张力十足，沉浸感强烈。评论者认为专辑缺少一个绝对的高潮点，但这并不妨碍它作为一张优秀作品的成立。整体而言，这是一张在死亡工业与暗黑氛围领域完成度较高的跨界实验之作。

items.body: New Jersey’s multifaceted world of underground music features a healthy amount of experimental jazz, mutating into various new and unique directions. In the same land that spawned Wayne Shorter, Sarah Vaughan and the famed Van Gelder studios, there seems to be an endless amount of artists pushing the boundaries on the genre today, from the hallucinatory prog-funk fusion of New Brunswick’s Guesstimate and Asbury Park’s We Used to Cut the Grass, to the improvisatory adventurousness of Paterson’s Thieves in Paris. Yet one name that always seems to appear while discussing the current state of Jersey jazz, and that is Mike Noordzy. From projects like El Noordzo, Mothguts and the Mike Noordzy Quintet, the Middlesex County-dwelling multi-instrumentalist never ceases to wow and amaze with his genre-defying sounds and unorthodox approaches. One of my favorite of his many albums was the shadowy avant-jazz soundscape that is Shark Funeral Songbook, released under his Noordzo moniker back in 2017. Nearly ten years later, he’s released a follow up, Shark Funeral Songbook Vol. 2, and it defied the odds and outshines the original. The album squirms and throbs with murky life, as it swings from percussion and string-based tracks that echo the works of Moondog, to surreal noir drifts and cataclysmic jazz-metal sludge and beyond. The album is a deep and varied collage of all kinds of styles and flavors, often blending and clashing together within a single track. The end result may offer hints of the likes of Tom Waits, Peter Brötzmann and, in the case of the harder tracks, Noordzy’s own Mothguts project, yet there is really no other album quite like this one. Between the collision of disparate genres, greasy textures, gritty atmospherics and unhinged rhythms all bleeding together within a very musique concrète-styled mix, this is a truly one-of-a-kind musical experience. The more you listen to this spooky record, the more you get pulled into its vastly immersive sonic world, and the more you feel like you’re getting a glimpse into the busy mind of a multifaceted artist who can channel their creativity into a thousand different directions at a moment’s notice. Boundless, unpredicatble and endlessly entertaining, Shark Funeral Songbook vol. 2 is a must have for fans of Sonny Sharrock, Colin Stetson and Moor Mother. Click here to get your copy today for Bandcamp Friday! -KH

items.body: When John Coltrane died in 1967 the jazz world felt a startling void. With the release of Expression , Coltrane’s final studio album, it must have felt like a narrative had been cut short of its intended ending. After all, unless Trane had recorded material that had never been released, that was it: no more new music from John Coltrane. We know the story 100 years after Trane’s birth, however. And did he ever record material that had yet to be released! Alice Coltrane worked relentlessly to preserve John’s towering musical legacy, and we know from Andy Beta’s incisive book on her life that after a long day of raising four children on her own, she would put the kids to bed, sit in meditation, and practice the music that meant so much to her and her late husband. What she also did was listen to unreleased recordings by John and prepare them for release. Among the recordings made public in the immediate years following John’s passing were two absolutely stunning (I can’t emphasize this word enough– stunning! ) recordings by the famed Classic Quartet of Trane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones: Transition in 1970 and Sun Ship in 1971. Transition McCoy Tyner related to writer David Wild that sometimes John would give them two notes, or maybe just a scale, as the basis of a composition before they recorded. The title track to the album Transition, recorded in the spring of 1965 , certainly could be such a piece. The work features a tightly focused quartet that absolutely opens up the gates and begins to tear down the fences. “Transition” is one the group’s wildest, most ferociously open pieces. It’s as though the catalytic power of Ascension or Om has been concentrated into a narrow and controlled conduit. Both the kinetic energy coursing through that conduit and the narrowness of the channel itself create the conditions for tension and combustion. The “Prayer and Meditation Suite,” on the other hand, is an absolute masterwork. I am of the persuasion that comparing works of Trane to other periods in his life can dangerously undervalue some of his accomplishments. Any suite, be it Meditations or “Prayer and Meditation” would beg comparison with A Love Supreme . Forget all that. “Prayer and Meditation” would stand as one the great works in the jazz canon if it were the only piece Coltrane and the Quartet created. Movement II: “Peace and After” is the sound of a quest for peace complete with all the pain inherent in that search. Movement IV: “Affirmation” picks up where “Transition” left off and rings with crisis, explosiveness, and spiritual urgency. Violence was always slinking nearby during Coltrane’s life, as it is for us today, and his music embraces this reality, but I would never describe his music as “violent.” Just note the third remaining song on Transition : “Dear Lord.” It is hard for me to imagine there ever existed a world without this vulnerable dedication to peace. Urgency and catharsis. Peace and vulnerability. The circumstances without and the transition within. Sun Ship In the nighttime hours of August 26, 1965, John Coltrane and his classic quartet walked into an East Manhattan studio. That year Martin Luther King and hundreds of peaceful protestors were arrested in Selma for wanting voter registration fairness. Malcolm X was shot to death. The first massive contingent of US ground troops landed in Vietnam, and the United States would slaughter tens of thousands of people before the year ended using machine guns and missiles fired from military jets. In Los Angeles, unemployment rates for black Americans grew to levels greater than during the Great Depression, housing discrimination was bolstered by law, and Watts exploded in rioting after a violent encounter between police and a black man. John Coltrane placed his mouth around his horn and blew. The sound that emerged, a passage of lyrical melody deeply tender and filled with solace, titled “Dearly Beloved,” lifted into the air. John embodied serenity and the path to it. People were dying and being denied their humanity by a power structure that required their destruction, and John never pretended this was not the case. The path to peace traveled through pain, not around it. People are dying right now as you read this, but life’s powerful play goes on, in all of its tragedy and real joy. Afterall, John’s baby boy Ravi had just been born, and John had assembled this collection of musicians to record at night because that day he was busy celebrating his first son, John Jr. 's, first birthday. Attaining does not come without suffering, but it also arrives with beauty. Attaining. Sun Ship. Ascent. Amen. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了Coltrane经典四重奏1965年春的录音，由Impulse!发行于1970和1971年。《Transition》标题曲体现了乐队将自由能量高度浓缩于紧密通道中的爆发力，演奏狂野而克制。《Prayer and Meditation Suite》被视为四重奏的杰作，第二乐章Peace and After呈现对宁静的探索，第四乐章Affirmation则充满危机感与精神紧迫性。Dear Lord作为脆弱而真诚的和平祈祷，兼具紧迫感与宣泄性。Alice Coltrane在John去世后系统整理未发行录音，使这些作品得以面世，展现了Coltrane在生命最后阶段对精神性与自由即兴的极致探索。

items.body: Felice Sciorilli first graced our pages last spring, appearing on Biodiversità Records’ 14 Soundcapes with the track “Breaths.” At the time, we recognized the unique nature of the piece, capturing the sound of “air pushed through the Etruscan sandstone cliffs by the incoming waves.” “Breaths” appears on Distant Places as well, a worthy inclusion. In a way, the album title is a misnomer. These places are not necessarily geographically distant; most come from the intertidal zone of the Tyrrhenian Sea. But as Sciorilli has a particular fascination with tide pools – some only centimeters deep – these sounds may be regarded as distant as most people seldom if ever encounter their nuances. When one hears that an album is recorded at the coast, one expects to hear a bevy of predictable material: wind and waves, gulls and other fair-weather fowls. These make appearances, but are not primary. Instead, Sciorilli concentrates on micro-sounds made macro. In “E,” water rushes into crevasses before spurting back out, powered by the force of the waves, although this is not technically the sound of the waves. Instead, this is the sound of waves in rocks, familiar to jetty walkers. As the angles of approach vary, so do the timbres. The tide pools first come into focus in the opening segment of “Cluster,” with a sound akin to the crackle of brine shrimp. The piece develops in movements, like the “Bohemian Rhapsody” of field recording. Soon there are crashing waves, then fizzes and pops, and finally the sound of pebbles tossing, turning, rolling back to the sea. “Bolle” and “Bubbles drift upward into the water” occupy different areas of the album while also being separated by tone. While hearing them, one recalls pablo diserens’ “The Shrinking Glacier” from last year’s ebbing ice lines, providing one with the opportunity to compare “healthy” bubbles with “unhealthy” bubbles, or bubbles that belong to a cycle with those escaping for the last time. The second piece is more effervescent, like alien birds swimming in soda; without hydrophones, one might never encounter such distant sounds. While listening, one is amazed by the number of musical parallels that can be found in nature: the quickening tempos of “From the Tidal Edge,” the glissandos of “Outflow.” Distant Places serves as a reminder that music imitates nature, not (save for starlings) the other way around. The set builds to the eighteen-minute centerpiece “Tiny Worlds,” a longer, reworked version of a piece that made the shortlist of The Radiophonic Broadcast’s Sounds of the Year 2025-26. Recorded in a tidal pool six centimeters deep (shown in the pdf that accompanies the download), the piece demonstrates just how rich, dense and diverse a micro-world can be, although to be fair, to the local Littorina snails there also exist micro-worlds within micro-worlds, from bacteria down to the smallest atom, each with a corresponding biophony. The “characters” that appear may be animate or inanimate, but each possesses a personality of its own: squeaking and whistling, popping and percolating. In the final piece, Sciorilli draws back from the water and embeds his microphone in the sand, muffling the sound of the nearby waves. “Under the Sand” operates as a parable. Sonic treasures are available everywhere, yet most of us never hear them; it is as if we too are buried in the sand, listening through wax and debris, treating micro-worlds as distant places although they are right beneath our feet. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑专注于意大利第勒尼安海潮间带的微观声音世界，录音集中在极浅的潮池之中。艺术家将水流入岩石缝隙的声音、卤水虾的噼啪声、气泡上升的嘶响等微观声响放大呈现，并借助水听器捕捉人耳通常无法感知的潜逃频段。作品结构呈现多乐章式发展，从细碎气泡逐步过渡到浪涌与砾石翻滚，十八分钟的核心曲目在一个仅六厘米深的潮池中完成录音，展现出微观环境中丰富的声学密度与层次。与其他类似主题的作品相比，此处的'健康'气泡与'濒死'气泡形成了耐人寻味的对照，提示自然循环中的声学差异。整体制作具有田野录音与声音艺术的鲜明意识。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It is always good to blend humor with strong influences, and right from the opening track of their debut album, "Lambo No. 5," a play on the famous "Mambo", Rokost draws on inspirations ranging from Dave Douglas and his "ethnic" trumpet style to Miles Davis and the use of special effects to create unique sonic textures. At times, the music seems to venture into psychedelic territory without ever losing its infectious, frenetic rhythm. Later, Marta Winnitzki's Rhodes piano (she also plays synthesizers) introduces mid-tempo passages that shift the rhythm, though the original melody, driven by Michel Schroeder's trumpet, always returns. This Hamburg-based quartet plays with time signatures and reimagines them; we recognize the conventions of classic jazz-rock while sensing them being pushed beyond their limits, not to abandon the genre, but to "expand the battlefield," to borrow a phrase from Michel Houellebecq.Menschenfeind evokes a space-age atmosphere, yet in its own unique way, distinct from the past, though nods to that era remain. Synthesizers dart back and forth reminiscent of the 70s, while the trumpet and keyboards establish a more contemporary setting where the two elements collide. This is where the term "symphonic jazz" applies, not due to pomp or grandiosity, but because of the interplay between the keyboards and the bass-and-trumpet foundation, with the latter instruments taking their own solos."Trotz" is dissonant and syncopated until a driving rhythm, so electric it borders on electronic, builds in intensity; its staccato breaks are slightly reminiscent of Bill Bruford's Earthworks. At times, one gets the impression that if Miles Davis were still with us, he might be creating something akin to the track "Jazon Hunter Strikes Again!"; much like the brilliant Japanese pianist Hiromi Uehara, her admiration for the 1970s drives a fusion of contemporary avant-garde with classic progressive elements, dreamy synthesizers, sophisticated trumpet lines, and a floating groove. Here, the sounds of the 70s, 80s, and 90s, along with techno, blend into a pastiche that serves as both homage and a gateway to the dreamlike "Meloda," a piece where electronic music once again takes on a progressive character within a jazz context."Attitude Adjustment" has a full-on rock rhythm, guitars aren't needed; as Weather Report so aptly demonstrated, the timing comes from elsewhere. A distorted synthesizer creates just the right kind of confusion to scramble the senses, while the bass and drums hammer out their parts, underpinning solos that scale mountains and swim through rivers, pumping adrenaline into those greens and fruits, produce as organic as this musical concept itself, where the artificial element pulses with more life than ever."We Will Still Be Here Tomorrow" is split in two; a classical trumpet shifts into a Baroque style while something very modern emerges from the seemingly disjointed drum beats. Yet, just when there might be a moment of coherence and composure, "Lines & Crimes" introduces a disorder that nonetheless encompasses melody and meaning, for this instrumental music seems to tell a story. The keyboards go wild, while the trumpet wails in increasingly piercing, high-pitched tones. "The Machines That Walk At Midnight" is almost industrial in its mechanical rhythm, yet there is genuine feeling when the bass kicks in; the electronic element has permeated not just the sound but the composition itself. Amidst this, Michel Schroeder adds a warm, magical touch on the trumpet, playing with effortless class and style, to remind us that this spirit doesn't subtract or lose anything, but rather adds to and elevates the music.Continuing the metaphor linking Rokost's music to Houellebecq's literature, one could say that the elementary particles of the fusion are present here but developing independently; they continue to evolve, triggering the release of substances like serotonin, the neurotransmitter that relays messages between nerve cells and helps regulate various bodily functions.The map and the territory are already laid out on the table, exposed; now it is simply a matter of submission to the possibility of an island... where all these molecules arrive and rearrange themselves, ultimately altering matter.

items._cn_summary: 这是汉堡四人组 ROKOST 的首张专辑，将幽默感与多元影响融为一体。乐评指出乐队以 Dave Douglas 的民族化小号语汇和 Miles Davis 的效果器手法为基础，在爵士摇滚框架内进行大胆实验：Rhodes 钢琴与合成器切换节奏重心，切分与不协和音在电气化节奏驱动下获得推进力，70/80/90 年代的声音与 techno 元素拼贴成既致敬又独立的整体。某些段落呈现太空时代氛围，另一些则像 Weather Report 那样在无吉他条件下构建全摇滚律动，失真合成器制造感官错乱。古典小号与巴洛克风格的拼贴、以及当代前卫元素与经典 progressive 的融合，使作品在爵士、电子、前卫摇滚之间持续游走。

items.body: This new album by Alessandro Tedeschi—better known by his sonic alter ego, Netherworld—is a remarkable work. Quite by chance, thanks to his young daughter, he stumbled upon old recordings dating back more than twenty years. These were recordings he had all but forgotten. Upon rediscovering them and realizing that their atmosphere perfectly matched the dark, sombre period he had been going through in recent months, he decided to revisit and rework material that no one had ever heard before. You could quite rightly call these Netherworld’s earliest experiments. Seven tracks were salvaged and restored. They fit seamlessly into the concept of Glacial Movements—Alessandro’s own label—leaving a profound, icy impression through their Ambient and Cinematic sound. We discover a Soundscape created—and, above all, inspired—by early expeditions to the North Pole. Distinctive field recordings echo through the metallic tones. You sense the imaginary presence of malevolent forces watching you, potentially pushing you towards a state of paranoia; you experience a sense of evil and an invisible presence that relentlessly pursues you. This effect is achieved simply through the power of the compositions, which, in my opinion, might well be hailed as Netherworld’s finest work. The sound is authentic and archaic, with deep, dominating tones that hit their mark with undeniable impact. It is hardly surprising, then, that the only track that failed to fully captivate me was the most ethereal one on the album. When music becomes an expression of dark thoughts, an artist is often at their most inspired—a fact perfectly embodied by the evocative title, “The Hermit”. (Rating:8). Listen to “Loneliness”: Loneliness by Netherworld About Netherworld Netherworld is the moniker of Alessandro Tedeschi, an Italian ambient and dark ambient composer based in Rome. The project is released through Tedeschi’s own label Glacial Movements, which he founded in 2006; “The Hermit” marks the label’s 20th anniversary. Netherworld’s music draws on manipulated fragments of classical music and field recordings, including ice masses, aurora-related material and Arctic wind recordings. Before focusing on Glacial Movements, the project released music through labels including Fario, Angle Rec, Umbra and Taalem. “Eternal Frost”, recorded in 2004, was originally issued by Umbra in a hand-numbered edition of 99 copies and later appeared on Bandcamp in February 2022. The Glacial Movements catalogue includes “Mørketid” (2007), “Over The Summit” (2011) and “Alchemy Of Ice” (2013, Tedeschi’s tenth full-length release). In 2017, Netherworld collaborated with Eraldo Bernocchi on “Himuro” for the label’s Iceberg Series. “Algida Bellezza” followed in 2019, and Side-Line’s interview with Netherworld was built around that release. “Vanishing Lands” appeared in 2022 and the Bvdub collaboration “Equilibrium” in 2023. “The Hermit” returns to material recorded before Glacial Movements existed: seven tracks salvaged from deteriorated CD-Rs and Minidiscs recorded in 2004.

items._cn_summary: 意大利作曲家Netherworld（Alessandro Tedeschi）意外发现二十余年前尘封的录音素材，将其修复重制后以《The Hermit》为名发行，恰好契合他近期的低沉心境。七首曲目贯穿北极探险主题，冰层极光与寒风等实地录音与金属质感音色交织，营造出寒冷压迫的氛围，隐约可感知某种恶意的无形存在。评论指出其音色古朴、深沉而具支配力，堪称Netherworld最佳作品之一；唯一未被完全吸引的是最缥缈的一首。该专辑亦是其自创厂牌Glacial Movements成立二十周年的纪念之作，呼应了从更早期实验回归当下的脉络。

items.body: So much has been written about John Coltrane and he's such a widely acknowledged and worshiped figure - one of jazz's top two most iconic artists, along with his once employer Miles Davis - that I don't feel I have anything new to bring to the table. Asked to comment on a favorite Coltrane album, however, I comply, for what it's worth. The first Coltrane album I purchased - a secondhand 1987 CD release - was Live at the Village Vanguard Again , recorded May 28, 1966. Prior to this, I had only heard Coltrane on Miles Davis' Kind of Blue . Village Vanguard Again was a punch in the gut, a puzzle for the mind and the record that won me over to free jazz for good, although it didn't happen overnight. I initially didn't understand what was going on, what to make of it. But was soon repeatedly attracted by the unhinged, torrential sounds unleashed on lengthy versions of "Naima" (a tender ballad with exquisite chords, here exuding rage and sorrow) and "My Favorite Things" (a distinctly lighthearted song from the movie "The Sound of Music", here given a terminally outrageous, or wonderfully out there treatment, according to your inclinations) interspersed with a six-minutes Jimmy Garrison bass solo. Each time I pressed the play button, I was unable to stop listening until the end of the total running time. The album held some arcane truth I couldn't live without anymore. It was music I had to sort out for myself, keep to myself, not music I could share with friends or relatives, let alone spin at parties... The line up had Alice Coltrane on piano, Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and flute, Rashied Ali on drums, with Coltrane on tenor, soprano and bass clarinet. I was unaware there was a much-loved Coltrane "classic quartet" then, and that this was not it! Some of the Impulse! catalogue was being reissued at that time (the mid-90s), Sanders' "Tauhid" and "Karma" among the batch, both also expanding my musical outlook. Coltrane's albums and archival releases were dropping in quick succession, each new one a mandatory listen. I stumbled on small-priced, worn out LP copies of "Transition" and "Kulu Se Mama" (both recorded in 1965). I was hooked, although none of those albums, and no other Coltrane record I heard after the 1966 live set, had the same definitive, life-altering effect, or reached the same high as that first exposure to the work. Could it be that I had started with a peak, a logical conclusion to what had come before? The music was equal parts perplexing, intimidating, meaningful, dark, luminous, an unrelenting war machine yet brimming with sensitivity, not quite inviting if you were not ready to surrender to its revolutionary approach, but fully uplifting and cleansing if you were. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / avant-garde / spiritual jazz / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是约翰·柯川1966年在Village Vanguard的现场录音，演绎了极长版本的《Naima》与《My Favorite Things》。演出阵容包含Alice Coltrane钢琴、Pharoah Sanders次中音萨克斯与长笛、Rashied Ali鼓手，以及柯川本人的次中音、高音及低音单簧管。作品呈现出狂放、暴雨般的自由即兴特质，将原本温柔的爵士标准曲彻底解构，融入愤怒与悲怆的情绪张力。低音单簧管的低沉音色、Jimmy Garrison六分钟的贝斯独奏，以及整体不受拘束的能量释放，使专辑成为自由爵士发展史上的标志性文献。对于尚未接触自由爵士的聆听者，这是一道需要主动臣服的门槛；而对那些愿意沉浸其中的人，音乐本身会带来净化与升华的力量。

items.body: Monument Builders, the latest release from Loscil, drops the temperature. The arctic melodies have been caught in a blast of sub-zero air, while their dense, deep textures are recognizable signatures within the Canadian artists’ style. Scott Morgan’s icy, ambient-tinted textures hang from the electronic notes, glimmering like a covering of dawn frost. You can’t blame everything on the weather, but you can apportion most of it to the current climate of fear, murder, isolation and self-destruction. Loscil prefers a cooler approach, but something else is causing this cold spell. The album was largely created in Morgan’s century-old home in Vancouver, and while the disintegrating tones and failing pitches have been influenced by the mothering atmosphere, they’ve been influenced by other things, too – specifically an old VHS copy of the American experimental film Koyaanisqatsi, the anti-humanist writings of philosopher John Gray, and the aerial photography of Edward Burtynsky, the latter of which shines a light on the toxic effects of pollution and environmental destruction. Add these things together and the record becomes a sober spirit. The music turns a deeper shade of blue, blinking away its optimism and becoming beautifully solemn as it contemplates its own mortality. The music’s draining the colour out of the face, turning it pale and unresponsive and leaving behind a red tide in its wake. It’s going through a cold snap, but it’s still breathing; in fact, the colder temperatures highlight the breath, making it clearer than it’s ever been before, appearing as a concentrated cloud of condensation. Monument Builders was born and put together during such a cold snap, at a time when friends and family members were experiencing their own physical struggles and enduring illnesses. The music pays tribute to this fight, because in spite of the pain, the notes are constantly progressing, brave and resolute in their enduring love while in the midst of a terrible struggle themselves. The notes give off a cold, dense chill, hypnotic in their cycles and repetitive, steel-smooth frameworks. This is the lo-fi sound: music enveloped in the crackles and pops of disintegration, of tonal erasure through constant decay. There’s a temporary rubbing out of the self as the negative emotions start to sprout like toxic weeds; the music grows introspective and quiet, as if it needs time alone. The sound is a deep, contemplative thought arriving from a confused and lost area of the mind. Through lo-fi, the music itself turns to scattered ash, reflecting a smouldering environment as well as the venomous corruption of the climate. The music is more pessimistic than it used to be, but it’s really realistic. Tired-sounding horns and harmonies are washed in waves of fatigue. The decay is a stark reminder of impermanence. Monument Builders grapples with mortality and massacre, a dangerous instability within the fragile order of all things. The music is stark and the punch has to strike at the gut in order for it to be an effective wake-up call, because much of the world is still fast asleep. As a warning, it blares louder than any siren. Some of the sounds are sinister, like in ‘Straw Dogs’, while others are pale souls drifting through the torched remains of an old hometown during the apocalypse. The slower tempo invites you to become more mindful of the space. The music is like a bird’s-eye-view of a place ravaged by an outbreak of war. Not a cold war – one that sets the sky on fire. Smoky plumes sail across the sky as the process of deforestation grips the music. Trees are being slaughtered on the orders of the government. The chainsaws and drills are dissonant instruments that highlight an absence of respect. Nature is being evicted, and her inhabitants shriek and cry, becoming the latest in a long line of refugees who have no choice but to flee an unwanted conflict; an endless cycle that begins with a dull ache and ends in a sharp blade of pain. Is hope really a weakness – a safety net, a coping mechanism, a chain? Or is it a sign of strength? Whatever it is, it’s the only thing that we have left. The reclaiming weeds are the only things that survive, but at least they’re still there. And so, the album closes on a bittersweet note, walking over the cracks in the pavement, ticking like an old metronome that has lost its time, swaying between destruction and revival. The higher notes are like aerial shots, spreading seeds that populate new areas in the sound and filling the music with the emergence of new life. As long as you’re breathing, there’s more right with you than there is wrong, I guess. www.kranky.net
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由加拿大电子音乐人Loscil在温哥华百年老宅中创作完成，融合了VHS录像带实验影像、哲学文本与航拍摄影的多重影响。整张作品以冰冷的氛围音色为核心，深沉的电子音景中融入颗粒感与噪音裂痕，声音材料呈现出缓慢消解的质感。音乐在反复循环与渐进推进之间形成沉思性的张力，低保真制作带来如灰烬散落般的听觉画面。专辑直面死亡、环境污染与人类自我毁灭的主题，音符却在困苦中展现出坚韧的尊严与持续的爱。整体风格沉郁而克制，冷色调的电子氛围兼具实验性与情感深度。

items.body: Birdsong, shifting ssshhhh, guitar string ping: rarely is it so immediately clear how the perception of things affects the perception of other things happening in the same space, in the same moment. And yet these musical events were not concurrent at the moment they were recorded to disk, even though they became so later, at the moment of playback; nor did their performers have any idea of what their collaborators would be performing. At the request of Melange Edition curator Ryoko Akama, three composers (Michael Pisaro, lo wie, and Manfred Werder) sent three scores each to three performers (Angharad Davies, Cristián Alvear, and d’incise), who picked three scores at random and recorded them without being aware of the choices made by the other performers. The three sets of three recordings were then overlaid by Akama to create three new pieces. Didn’t that string just ping in reflective response to that electronic chirp? Didn’t Alvear just pause what sounded like an attack on his guitar with a chisel to let Davies intone a group of letters, her voice cracking slightly on the last letter in anticipation of the bowl d’incise is about to drag across a stone floor? No, they couldn’t have heard one another. Their dots are scattered according to separate logics, any lines between them being drawn purely in the ear of the listener, like the alignments of aural constellations in a sky of silence. It’s as if causality is an illusion. Though the project participants all stress in the liner notes their trust in Akama, they each admit to being amazed by the quality and musicality of the outcomes, and with good reason: each track simply sounds like good music. The work is based on a willingness to throw things wide open to a range of possibilities and to trust in the senses of listeners, rather than the laws of any musical tradition or theory of harmony or melody, to sort things out. That such a strategy so often produces pleasing and enthralling results points to the ways in which our brains seem predisposed to seek and find coherence, even in the least promising of confuddlements. Similar propensities for joining the metaphorical dots have been observed experimentally in all sorts of areas, from facial recognition to language acquisition. In fact, it’s possible that the whole of consciousness itself can be attributed to these sense-making practices, these habits of turning an apparently disparate jumble of stimuli into something resembling a world. Musings on the nature of consciousness seem like quite a departure from a music project such as “3 + 3 = 3”, but the relevant point is that the correspondences and coherences that emerge across the three pieces aren’t just happy coincidences. Rather, they are signs that everything is working as it should: that composers and performers and listeners are engaged in the collaborative act of making sense of things, separated by time and space and yet entangled somehow, such that each completes the others’ thoughts. In short, all the things needed for making music are present, even if centralised control and an overarching plan in the mind of one individual are not. There’s a powerful sense of communion in this, as well as discovery.     Michael Pisaro lo wie Manfred Werder Angharad Davies Cristián Alvear d’incise Melange Edition
items._genre: experimental / contemporary composition / sound art / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由策展人Ryoko Akama发起，三位作曲家（Pisaro、wie、Werder）各写了三份乐谱，三位演奏家（Davies、Alvear、d'incise）各自随机抽取一份独自录音，彼此不知对方选择。Akama随后将九段录音分三组叠加，形成三首新作品。评论指出，演奏家们实际无法相互听见，但叠加后产生的因果错觉——吉他的拨弦似乎在回应电子声鸣、小提琴的停顿似乎为让出人声空间——揭示了人类大脑天生倾向于在散乱刺激中建立连贯性与意义。这种感知的拼合本身就是一种协作行为。作品体现了极简框架下的开放性策略：不依赖传统和声或旋律法则，而是将意义生成完全交由听者的感官来完成。

items.body: BEAST (Birmingham ElectroAcoustic Sound Theatre) is a multichannel sound associated with the University of Birmingham’s Electroacoustic Music Studios,comprising of as many as 100 speakers. With these speakers encircling the audience, it’s possible to produce many spatial and acousmatic effects. What this often translates to in practice is a genre of music that leans heavily on fast, dynamic transitions between different kinds of sound and different positions in the aural field (that sphere around your head that establishes the distance up to which you can hear), and on sounds that uniformly impress when played on a multichannel sound system: bell-like sounds, rushing noise, and bass thumps, among several others. Many of my favourite pieces at BEAST FEaST 2016 eschewed this aesthetic, or rather subjected the most useful parts of it to different creative ideals. Ben Peers’ soothing, quiet drones were a welcome shift of mood from some of the more aggressive aural assaults perpetrated using the BEAST system, though the lower frequency rumble seemed added simply for the sake of acousmatic convention. In Emma Margetson’s ‘Tick’, the ticking of a metronome was shifted, splintered, and refracted in the temporal and spatial domains, with subtle pitched musical tones helping to imply the space through which the ticking moved. Annie Mahtani’s ‘Aeolian’ used quiet chords in its evocation of a quiet rainstorm and its aftermath; though her field recordings consisted of often-heard staples such as passing traffic, the magic of the piece lay in how these sounds were transformed by the dampness left by the rain (even the wind sounded different). Charlie Lockwood’s fairytale ambient musicboxes got progressively darker and grittier, before ending on an elegiac note. And Helene Hedsund’s ‘Bus No. 1’, as well as using bass to make the floor vibrate like that of a bus, also featured some nice harmonies that gradually unravelled into cacophony in a very pleasing way. Most of the above featured harmony of some sort or other, but some of the more surprising and striking pieces at the festival didn’t foreground harmony at all. I really liked Tsun Winston Yeung’s ‘Variations’, in which the composer’s EEG-measured brainwaves helped to control the sound as he meditated, read a book, did sums, and memorised text in an engaging piece of stagecraft. Another memorable performance came from Kosmas Giannoutakis, who periodically left the grand piano he was playing to walk round the circle of speakers surrounding the audience, while algorithms took the piano sounds and spun them into dense echoing textures. Luca Danieli’s ‘La Tabula Rasa’ used manipulated, machine-like spoken voice and a dose of grim humour to relate the loneliness and abjection of a web server buried deep in a network. I was probably the only person in the Elgar Concert Hall who wasn’t blown away by Jonty Harrison’s concert-length ‘Going / Places’. This long series of aural postcards, fractured and remoulded using the usual acousmatic devices, somehow failed to remind me of the experience of being in any place in particular, except perhaps in a hall surrounded by speakers at an acousmatic music concert. Barry Truax’s ‘Pendledrøm’, on the other hand, effectively conveyed the impression of a commute through Copenhagen, in which the weary commuter is half-aware of her familiar, routine surroundings and half drifting along in a dreamlike state. As I realised during Margetson’s piece, it’s primarily by means of harmony that sounds are linked to space, much as time and space are linked by way of memory. The fact that explicit harmony is by no means essential to the transportative effects of music suggests that the former is only a smoke that both announces and obscures some other fire. Alexander Pospischil, ‘Ichi-Kousatsu’ The installations at this year’s BEAST FEaST were fantastic. In John Kefala Kerr’s ‘Book of Bells’, the visitor was invited to locate passages from various antique books in order to complete a word search, ringing a different bell each time a passage is completed. In the background was a soundtrack featuring more bells and a cathedral choir. It was fun to do this task at the same time as other people, their bells ringing out at unexpected moments as I scanned yellow pages for sound references. Alexander Pospischil’s ‘Ichi-Kousatsu’ also required visitor participation, in the form of a chair positioned between a hanging tree branch and its shadow on the wall cast by the light from a projector. When I sat on the chair, branches began growing and budding out of my shadow, allowing me to experience, in a butoh-esque way, a sort of becoming-tree. The knocking together of branches in the wind in the installation’s audio component added to the overall effect. It was recently reported that scientists have discovered a discrete region of the brain that is activated when hearing music, and only when hearing music (not when hearing barking dogs, crackling fires, or any other sound). I wonder during how many pieces at BEAST FEaST the neurons in this part of my brain forgot to fire, or fired when they weren’t supposed to. Not everyone making work for sound systems such as BEAST thinks of what they do as ‘music’ in the traditional (neurological?) sense, but I found that the pieces that most engaged me, as a non-specialist member of the general public, were the ones that more clearly embraced musicality of some recognisable form or another. If the aim is to grow and broaden the horizons of this work in order to appeal to a wider audience and diversify its pool of practitioners, this may be one way to go. BEAST Cover image: BEAST tweeter arrays in the Elgar concert hall
items._cn_summary: 本文评述了2016年BEAST FEaST音乐节的多声道电声作品。BEAST系统使用多达100个扬声器环绕观众，通过空间与声学效果创造沉浸式听觉体验。文章逐一分析了多首参展作品：Ben Peers的柔和低频嗡鸣、Emma Margetson《Tick》对节拍器声音在时域与空域中的碎片化折射、Annie Mahtani《Aeolian》以雨天环境录音为核心的声音变换、Charlie Lockwood渐趋黑暗的音乐盒氛围、Hélène Hedsund《Bus No. 1》模拟公交车地板震动的低频处理。Tsun Winston Yeung《Variations》以脑电波数据控制声音合成的舞台呈现极具新意，Kosmas Giannoutakis将钢琴声经算法转化为致密回响织体，Luca Danieli《La Tabula Rasa》以机器化人声表达网络服务器的孤寂。整体聚焦于电声音乐中空间化处理、现场演出与声音艺术的融合路径。
